Is this real or Fake? Examining the effects of disclosure of AI-generated content and source type in instagram-based travel destination advertising on consumer attitudes and behavioral intentions
abstract: The current research investigates the effects of disclosure (versus non-disclosure) of AI-generated content and source type in travel destination-related advertising posts on consumers' attitudes and behavioral intentions. Study 1 ( N = 395) examined how AI disclosure effects on consumer responses varied across four source types (business versus government organization versus non-government organization versus social media influencer). In Study 2 ( N = 201), we investigated the effects of human social media influencers posting AI-generated content with or without disclosure. We found evidence for the effectiveness of the disclosure in recognizing the AI-generated content for the advertising posts by a hospitality business and social media influencers. Disclosing the AI-generated origin of social media influencers' advertising posts lowered brand credibility, attitude, and purchase intention. Attitudes towards AI moderate the relation between the recognition of the AI origin of the post and brand credibility. • Disclosure of AI-generated social media advertising posts contributes to the recognition of the AI origin in the case of the hotel and of social media influencers. • Disclosure of AI-generated social media advertising posts by influencers lowered brand credibility and attitude. • The recognition of AI-generated social media influencers advertising posts negatively affects brand credibility, attitude, and purchase intentions. • In the case of social media influencers, consumers' attitudes towards AI moderate the relationship between the recognition of the post's AI origin and brand credibility.

title: Beyond the ideal: How 'Instagram vs reality' content shapes positive and negative body image
abstract: Body-positive content on social media has been found to have positive consequences for body image. However, research on the mechanisms underlying this effect is scarce. Based on the tripartite influence model (Thompson et al., 1999) and acceptance model of intuitive eating (Avalos & Tylka, 2006), this study examined the role of four possible mechanisms: appearance-comparison, thin-ideal internalization, body acceptance by others, and internal body orientation. Young women (18-30 years, Mage = 24.42, N = 340) were randomly assigned to view appearance-ideal, body-positive (Instagram vs. reality), or appearance-neutral content. Before and after the manipulation, indicators of negative and positive body image were assessed, as well as the four possible mechanisms under consideration. A series of ANCOVAs and paired sample t-tests revealed that exposure to body-positive content has a positive impact on positive body image compared to the other two conditions. Exposure to body-positive content was also found to result in a decrease of thin-ideal internalization. Moreover, while no significant differences were observed between conditions at posttest, body appreciation by others and internal body orientation showed selective within-condition increases from pretest to posttest in the body-positive condition with effects for internal body orientation limited to one indicator. These findings suggest that reductions in thin-ideal internalization and, to a lesser extent, increases in body appreciation by others and internal body orientation, may be mechanisms underlying the impact of body-positive content on body image.

title: Immersive virtual reality for caregivers of children and adolescents with ADHD: A mixed-methods study of stress reduction, empathy engagement, and quality of life outcomes
abstract: Caregivers of children and adolescents with ADHD experience significant psychological and practical burdens. However, existing support interventions often lack experiential and flexible components. This mixed-methods study evaluated the feasibility and within-person changes associated with an immersive virtual reality (VR) intervention in addressing stress, empathy engagement patterns, and perceived quality of life among caregivers of individuals aged 5–18 with ADHD. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. Three hundred and fifty caregivers participated in an eight-session VR program alternating between stress management (nature immersion) and empathy-focused (ADHD simulation and practical strategies) modules. Quantitative outcomes, including the Perceived Stress Scale, Toronto Empathy Questionnaire, and WHOQOL-BREF, were assessed at four time points. Qualitative data were collected via interviews and focus groups. Generalized estimating equation analyses revealed significant reductions in stress; however, changes in empathy engagement were only transient and observed during the active phase, with these gains not sustained at the one-month follow-up. Minimal changes were observed in quality of life across the assessment points, indicating that the intervention’s impact was largely domain-specific rather than broadly transformative. Qualitative themes highlighted immersive escape, rapid stress relief, and increased subjective understanding, but also identified barriers related to technology, content realism, and sustainability of empathy engagement gains. Immersive VR interventions demonstrate high feasibility and offer substantial, rapid stress reduction for caregivers of youth with ADHD and moderate, short-term empathy engagement. Design improvements and ongoing exposure may be required for sustained empathy engagement and broader quality of life benefits. • VR intervention reduced stress in ADHD caregivers by 27% post-intervention. • Empathy rose during VR training but declined after the program ended. • Brief VR nature sessions offered rapid relief for time-constrained caregivers. • Qualitative findings revealed immersive escape and enhanced understanding of ADHD. • VR and peer support boosted caregiver engagement and satisfaction.

title: Internet use, social isolation, and loneliness among older adults: A multi-wave analysis
abstract: This study investigated the longitudinal relationship between the frequency of internet use and loneliness in older adults in the UK, considering perceived social isolation. Data were obtained from Waves 9-14 of the UK Household Longitudinal Study. Linear mixed models were employed to examine the association between internet use, loneliness, and social isolation over time. The analytical sample comprised 13,704 adults aged 65 and above. The models controlled for sociodemographic and health-related covariates. The results suggested that infrequent internet users (including those with no internet access) experienced higher levels of loneliness compared to frequent internet users, especially daily users. The associations persisted even after adjusting the models for covariates. Participants who frequently felt socially isolated consistently reported the highest levels of loneliness, regardless of their level of digital engagement. A significant three-way interaction between wave, internet use, and social isolation revealed that differences between the socially isolated and non-isolated older adults were the largest during Waves 11-13 and narrowed by Wave 14. This shift may be an outcome of COVID-19, reflecting the pandemic’s lasting social impact. These findings support the Digital Divide framework. The frequency of internet use is associated with lower levels of loneliness in older adults who do not feel socially isolated; however, internet use alone may not be enough to fill the void of human interaction in those who feel socially isolated.

title: Blurring the boundaries of the self: Instagram's impact on bodily identity and multisensory experience among young adults
abstract: Social media use is believed to shift users' focus to the outer body (i.e., physical appearance).However, this perspective may simplify the relationship between social media use and body perception.This study aimed to extend current knowledge by examining how three Instagram usage variables (i.e., daily time spent on Instagram, years of Instagram use, and Instagram beauty filter use) affect not only body image, but also individuals' inner body perception (i.e., interoception) and the integration of internal and external bodily experiences (i.e., embodiment).A sample of 95 young adults (64% women; M age = 25.8 years, SD = 4.25) completed selfreported measures of social media usage and body image concerns, underwent a heartbeat tracking task for assessing cardiac interoceptive accuracy and confidence, and experienced two virtual reality-based body illusions assessing face and full-body embodiment.Following multiple linear regression analyses, no social media usage variables were significantly associated with body image concerns or interoception.However, years of Instagram use and Instagram beauty filter use were uniquely associated with heightened susceptibility to face and full-body embodiment, respectively.We hypothesized that prolonged Instagram use and exposure to idealized, homogenized appearance-focused content may blur the perceptual boundary between self and others, a central process to bodily identity.Over time, this could contribute to an erosion of bodily identity.These results highlight a novel pathway through which social media use may shape self-perception: not by altering body image but by disrupting the integration of internal and external bodily experiences.

title: A dual-component framework of interactive attention: Gaze markers of expertise and engagement in split-attention gameplay
abstract: Video games require complex coordination of motor skills and active perception, yet the cognitive mechanisms underlying the transition from novice to expert remain under-examined. This study utilizes a custom-built 2D puzzle-platformer, Vacillate, to investigate how game literacy moderates the distribution of visual attention in a split-attention environment. Using eye-tracking data from 52 participants, we identify a significant "attentional cost" in novice players, characterized by high foveal dependency and frequent avatar-monitoring. Conversely, increased expertise predicts visual economy, where players reallocate gaze toward predictive goal information. Results reveal that game literacy is a robust negative predictor of avatar-dwell time (R2=.334), while self-reported enjoyment is related to slower, more deliberate saccadic processing. This paper proposes a dual-component framework that suggests that in digital environments, user expertise is not defined by raw performance speed, but by the strategic economy of visual resources, a shift from foveal-reliance to predictive environmental scanning.

title: Identity manipulation in online grooming: Gendered strategies among male suspects
abstract: • The study reveals gender-specific patterns in the use of identity manipulation during online grooming. • The nuanced and varied use of identity deception highlights the urgent need for prevention programs to move beyond simplistic “stranger danger” messages toward scenario-based education that reflects the complexity of offender strategies. • For male victims, impersonation frequently functioned as a sexual access strategy that leverages heteronormative expectations to reduce resistance. • For female victims, identity deception often operated as a mechanism for building trust and emotional leverage, sometimes facilitating retaliatory or coercive behaviors.

title: Beyond the post: Effects of vividness dominance on attention and recall of visual misinformation on social media
Perceived effectiveness of online vigilantism: The role of schadenfreude and moral grandstanding
abstract: As online platforms increasingly become arenas for informal justice, understanding the psychological drivers of online vigilantism is paramount. This study investigates the predictive influence of Schadenfreude and moral grandstanding on the perceived effectiveness of online vigilantism, while examining how these mechanisms vary across levels of participation. Data were collected from a representative sample of 1,000 Korean adults through a proportional quota sampling method. Using a combination of ANOVA and multiple regression analysis with bootstrapping, the study reveals several key findings. First, a higher intensity of participation in online vigilantism correlates with a more positive perception of its effectiveness, suggesting a reinforcement loop driven by engagement. Second, Schadenfreude serves as a significant "affective fuel" across all groups, reinforcing the "emotionalization of justice" in digital spaces. Third, while prestige-seeking moral grandstanding drives the perception of effectiveness among active participants (the "performers"), dominance-seeking motives are more salient among non-participants (the "potential directors"). These findings suggest that online vigilantism has evolved into a socio-cultural spectacle where personal psychological rewards and identity performance often overshadow the pursuit of public justice. The study concludes with policy recommendations, including the implementation of "affective filtering" algorithms and tailored digital citizenship education.

title: Unraveling the behavioral and autonomic dynamics of defensive states in humans in an unconstrained, immersive virtual world
abstract: Defensive responses to threats are crucial for mental and physical health. Animal studies highlight different defense modes related to threat proximity, yet human defense dynamics remain underexplored due to experimental restrictions and oversimplification of research designs. The current multimodal study thus comprehensively characterized defense patterns in humans on the behavioral (movement speed, body, head, and eye rotations), autonomic (heart rate and skin conductance), and subjective level (perceived dread) in an immersive virtual reality environment. Ninety-four participants performed a foraging task while the context signaled varying levels of threat, that were also reflected in individual dread ratings. Upon relatively distal, ambiguous threat, (oculo)motor activity and heart rate decreased, reminiscent of freezing behaviors in rodents. While skin conductance levels increased when under (perceived) attack, heart rate unexpectedly decreased. Positive cross-correlations among movement metrics and autonomic measures as well as significant relationships of biobehavioral adjustments to successful coping behavior suggest the existence of circumscribed, adaptive defensive states that were further shaped by individual differences in anxiety and aggression. Overall, the current study offers valuable insights into the dynamic and integrated nature of defensive states in humans, while also establishing an ecologically valid research framework to advance translational research on threat processing across species.

title: When conversational AI personalises too much: Refining privacy calculus for bundled interactional cues in AI-mediated disclosure
Understanding the efficacy of online bystander intervention when journalists are the targets
abstract: Research on hate-based harassment often focuses on the role of bystanders, with the aim to increase awareness and the likelihood of intervention. As the domain for abuse has shifted from in-person to digital spaces, bystander interventions have been applied to online interactions. However, the assumption underlying this shift is that bystander interventions are efficacious online and that targets consent to intervention. Journalists, who are often required to be online for professional reasons, serve as a good test case for these assumptions as they are both more likely to endure online harassment and are more visible. To address the challenges related to designing interventions for online harassment, this project takes a co-design process approach in which in-depth interviews with journalists inform a set of modified interventions that are then validated on a second purposive sample of journalists who have been targeted. This approach produces data that centers journalists’ needs in the context of their unique experiences and thus, offers us important insights for designing online harassment interventions. Practically, this work offers a model for foregrounding the needs of communities of practice in design. Overall, this work has the potential to shift how we think of bystander interventions.

title: Longitudinal changes in gamers’ profiles and gaming disorder risk
abstract: Gaming engagement spans a continuum from non-problematic play to gaming disorder (GD). Although emotion regulation, motivations and mental health are established correlates of problematic gaming, less is known about how these factors co-occur within individuals and their influence on developmental trajectories. Using a large international sample of gamers (men, women, non-binary), across three waves over a 12-month period (T1: N = 5255; T2: N = 1926; T3: N = 2317), this study examined the stability of four psychological gamer profiles: Avoidant, Engaged, Relational, and Dysregulated, based on emotion regulation and motivational factors. Latent transition analysis was used to examine profile stability and transitions over time, incorporating time-varying covariates (gaming time and psychological distress). Regression analyses tested whether baseline profile membership predicted GD symptom severity one year later, beyond initial symptoms. Profiles showed high longitudinal stability, supporting their interpretation. Avoidant and Engaged profiles reflected adaptive patterns that differed primarily in motivational intensity. However, transitions from the Relational to the Dysregulated profiles were significantly predicted by higher psychological distress, while gaming time showed only modest associations with profile change. Importantly, baseline Relational and Dysregulated profiles predicted higher GD symptom severity at follow-up, independent of initial GD symptoms. These findings highlight the public mental health relevance of emotionally informed, person-centred approaches. Profilebased identification may support more accurate population screening, inform prevention strategies that avoid over-pathologizing high engagement, and guide stepped interventions aligned with ICD-11 criteria.

The role of anthropomorphized artificial intelligence in shaping consumer mental models and emotional experience in digital branding
abstract: The rapid emergence of anthropomorphized artificial intelligence (AI) in digital branding has transformed how consumers perceive, interpret, and emotionally engage with brand-mediated interactions. The study investigates how human-like cues embedded in AI-driven brand agents, such as conversational warmth, social presence, and adaptive responsiveness, shape consumers’ cognitive and affective processes. Drawing on theories of mind perception, appraisal-based emotion, and the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, a dual-pathway framework is proposed and empirically tested in which anthropomorphism influences brand outcomes through both mental model formation and emotional appraisal. A mixed-method design was employed, combining controlled experimental manipulations of AI anthropomorphism with survey data from 450 participants. Results from structural equation modeling (SEM) indicate that anthropomorphic AI significantly enhances mental model formation (β = 0.63, p < 0.001) and emotional responses (β = 0.58, p < 0.001), which in turn predict trust (β = 0.49, p < 0.001), satisfaction (β = 0.46, p < 0.001), and perceived brand authenticity (β = 0.41, p < 0.001). Multigroup analyses further reveal moderation effects: younger consumers exhibited stronger emotional engagement, while digitally literate participants relied more heavily on cognitive pathways. These findings highlight the evolving role of AI as a relational brand actor and underscore the importance of calibrated human-like design features in cultivating meaningful, trustworthy, and emotionally resonant digital brand experiences. The study advances theoretical understanding of consumer-AI interactions and provides actionable guidance for designing AI-driven touchpoints that foster sustainable engagement in contemporary branding ecosystems.

title: Corrigendum to ‘Corrigendum to ‘Can online behaviors be linked to mental health? Active versus passive social network usage on depression via envy and self-esteem’’ [Computers in Human Behavior 162 (2025) 108455, 172 (2025) 108744]
Why we feel regret and guilt about using digital technology in our free time – A European perspective
abstract: Despite the widespread use of digital technologies during free time and its potential benefits for wellbeing and recovery from work life, digital engagement is considered a low-quality form of free time that often results in significant regret and guilt. Given its increasing significance as an accessible source of relaxation and enjoyment in today’s post-COVID digitised society and the negative health consequences of chronic regret and guilt, the current study sought to explore the drivers of guilt and regret following digital free time across Europe. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 150 participants from Czechia, Germany, Poland, Spain, French-speaking Switzerland and the UK. A thematic analysis of the data showed that digital free time was perceived as inconsistent with the ideal of meaningful and self-determined free time and led to a spiral of guilty pleasure: Unintentional or involuntary uptake of digital activity, digital engagement beyond the desired duration and consumption of unwanted content were followed by a negative evaluation of one’s own digital behaviour as a self-regulative failure and digital free time as unproductive, passive, unhealthy and inauthentic. The perceived meaninglessness and lack of control over digital free time engendered feelings of guilt and regret, which were maintained through continued digital engagement during free time. Measures to reduce guilt and regret may require societal-level changes in the way digital technology use during free time is portrayed in media and mainstream discourse in combination with structural changes to digital entertainment apps or services.

Perceptions and adoption of AI in public relations: Innovation attributes, threats, and practical implications
abstract: This study examines how public relations professionals perceive the attributes of artificial intelligence (AI) innovation and related threats, and how these perceptions relate to their attitudes toward AI adoption and AI use at work. Using the Diffusion of Innovation theory as the primary framework, the research analyzes survey data from US-based public relations practitioners (N = 661). Findings emphasize the importance of aligning AI tools with existing public relations workflows and addressing user concerns to support effective, inclusive AI integration. This study offers theoretical and practical insights for advancing the adoption of AI in public relations practice.

title: Blessed or not? The dual-path influence mechanism of intelligent elderly care service robots' roles on Chinese family caregivers' well-being
Young people evaluating online information credibility. Special issue synthesis
abstract: In response to current threats of mis- and disinformation in the contemporary digital society, the special issue of Computers in Human Behaviors entitled “Young people evaluating online information credibility” aimed at uniting articles that address two research questions from a psychological and educational perspective: What kind of cognitive processes are responsible for accurate information credibility evaluation? How can such processes be initiated and supported? The invited papers concentrated on long-term cognitive processes, strategies, and training approaches integrated in educational contexts, rather than short-term processes in the laboratory. After providing a brief overview of the included papers, we address the question why such research is needed, for which we focus on the case of the annulled presidential elections 2024 in Romania that illustrates the consequences of disinformation on democratic societies. To conclude from a broader perspective, we describe two categories of interventions aimed at countering misinformation: protectionist interventions and empowering interventions. The latter category is illustrated by the papers included in this special issue.

title: How augmented reality usage traces shape consumer decision-making in online food shopping: The roles of virtual taste and contamination sensitivity
Adolescent bystanders in technology-facilitated sexual dating abuse: A latent class analysis
abstract: Adolescent bystander responses to technology-facilitated sexual dating abuse (TFSDA) and their associated factors remain understudied. This pioneering study applied latent class analysis to identify distinct profiles of adolescents’ bystander responses to TFSDA and examined, within the Action Coils Model of bystander intervention, the intra-individual, event-related, and post-intervention factors associated with each profile. Between February and May 2023, 322 adolescents (54.7% cisgender girls; M age =15.17, SD =1.65) from 25 schools in Portugal completed an online questionnaire. Four bystander profiles emerged: Victim-centered helpers (37%), Passive bystanders (32.6%), Comprehensive helpers (22.4%), and Ambivalent/Perpetrator-aligned bystanders (8.1%). Cisgender girls were more often Victim-centered and Comprehensive helpers , whereas boys tended to be Passive bystanders . Younger adolescents were more frequently Victim-centered helpers , while older adolescents were more often Comprehensive helpers . Sexual minority identification and personal experiences of technology-facilitated sexual victimization characterized Comprehensive helpers and Ambivalent/Perpetrator-aligned bystanders . Higher empathy distinguished Victim-centered and Comprehensive helpers , whereas recognition of TFSDA as inappropriate was greatest among Comprehensive helpers compared with Ambivalent/Perpetrator-aligned and Passive bystanders . Greater proactive actionism also characterized Comprehensive helpers . Identifying the victim as a cisgender girl and personally knowing the victim were more common among Victim-centered and Comprehensive helpers , whereas knowing the perpetrator was more frequent among Ambivalent/Perpetrator-aligned bystanders and not knowing those involved typified Passive bystanders . Attributing responsibility to the perpetrator and reporting sadness for the victim and anger toward the perpetrator were more common among Victim-centered and Comprehensive helpers than among Passive bystanders . Positive feelings following intervention were highest among Comprehensive helpers . Implications for prevention and intervention are discussed.

title: Combining intergroup contact and outgroup embodiment in virtual reality: An exploratory test of backfire and secondary transfer effects of outgroup embodiment
abstract: Weight stigma is a widespread issue with health and psychological consequences. Virtual reality offers a platform to integrate intergroup contact with outgroup embodiment to decrease stigma, yet little is known about whether effects extend beyond the target group, which we conceptualize as the secondary transfer effect of outgroup embodiment (STE-OE), or under what circumstances such interventions might backfire. This exploratory study examined whether embodying an avatar representing a person with obesity, combined with positive intergroup contact with a person with average weight, could reduce weight stigma. Participants (N = 63, Finland) were randomly assigned to the outgroup embodiment or control condition and completed a cooperative task in VR. Participants in the outgroup embodiment condition expressed colder explicit attitudes toward people with obesity compared to the control condition. Estimated condition differences in implicit attitudes varied as a function of self-esteem and perceived threat, such that outgroup embodiment was associated with more negative attitudes at lower levels of perceived threat and at higher levels of self-esteem, with the pattern reversing at higher threat and lower self-esteem. Colder attitudes toward people with obesity generalized to other stigmatized groups, providing initial evidence consistent with STE-OE in VR. Findings also suggest that the impact of VR-based interventions on outgroup attitudes may depend on individual characteristics and contextual perceptions. By documenting negative STE-OE and boundary conditions under which VR interventions may backfire, this study underscores both the potential and the risks of immersive technologies for intergroup relations research.

title: Trust erodes, fatigue builds: How prompt uncertainty traps users in recrafting loops
Online consent misread: A mixed-method study on (cyber)rape culture's influence on sexual consent perceptions and responses to unsolicited genital images
abstract: Objective This study examined how the victim’s sexual interest and the endorsement of cyber-sexual violence myths influence perceptions of sexual consent, victim blaming, and perceived severity in incidents involving unsolicited genital images (i.e., ‘dickpics’). By integrating Sexual Script Theory and Attribution Theory , the research aimed to clarify how individual beliefs interact with situational cues in shaping judgments about online sexual encounters. Method A mixed-methods design was employed with 521 active social media users from Spain. Participants completed measures of cyber-sexual violence myth acceptance and social desirability, then were randomly assigned to read a vignette depicting unsolicited genital image sharing, where the victim’s prior sexual interest was manipulated (interest vs. no interest). Quantitative ratings of victim blaming, perceived severity, and consent perceptions were collected, alongside qualitative written explanations of consent perceptions. Results Quantitative data analyses revealed that when the victim showed interest (vs. no interest), participants with stronger myth endorsement attributed greater consent to the victim and were more likely to interpret implicit cues as indicative of consent, which, in turn, was associated with increased victim blaming and lower perceived severity. Thematic and semantic network analyses replicated and extended prior findings, revealing how participants’ beliefs shaped their reasoning and how they organized multiple justifications for consent judgments. Conclusions These findings underscore the complex, context-dependent nature of sexual consent online and the critical role of preexisting myths in shaping judgments. Interventions should focus on challenging these myths and promoting awareness of implicit consent cues to reduce victim-blaming and misinterpretation in digital environments.

title: Empathy in leadership communication: Experimental evidence from two vignette studies on AI's role in message improvement and observers' perceptions
abstract: The increasing availability of generative AI tools raises the question of whether they can meaningfully support leadership communication. One use case discussed in the literature is AI’s potential to enhance empathetic communication. Yet little is known about whether leaders are willing to use AI’s support or how observers interpret such communication. This research examines the topic from two complementary perspectives using two vignette-based experiments with working adults in Germany. In Study 1, participants in the leadership scenario received advice framed as coming from an AI system or a human communication specialist before revising a previously written feedback email. We compared empathy levels of emails before and after giving advice to determine whether participants were willing to use AI advice. The likelihood of revising the email in response to the advice did not differ depending on the human vs. AI condition, nor did we find differences in terms of improvement of empathy. Study 2 investigated how observers interpreted leadership communication with varying degrees of AI involvement (no AI, low AI, and high AI). High AI use (generating the whole message with AI) led to lower evaluations of empathy, credibility, and feedback quality compared to the no-AI condition, whereas low AI use (using AI to fix wording) did not result in negative reactions. Tentative evidence suggests that AI literacy may mitigate the negative effect of high AI involvement on perceived empathy, but it did not moderate the effects on credibility or quality. Together, the findings show that while individuals were open to integrating AI advice when communicating in a leadership scenario, high AI involvement can negatively affect how observers interpret their messages.

title: Understanding the loneliness paradox of the digital age: Offline social support mediates the relationship between addictive social media use and loneliness – A gender comparison in the German general population
abstract: Never before has humanity been so well connected, and yet felt so alone, as in the digital age. The present study aimed to identify potential factors that could contribute to the explanation of this loneliness paradox. Therefore, the relationship between addictive social media use (SMU), perceived offline social support, and loneliness has been investigated in male and female persons. Data of 7,318 adult social media users (men: n = 3,579, women: n = 3,739; age in years: M = 47.72, SD = 15.22, range: 18–89) from the German general population were collected via an online survey. The current findings show the same result pattern for men and women. Addictive SMU was positively associated with loneliness, and both variables were negatively linked to offline social support; offline social support statistically mediated the association between addictive SMU and loneliness. Furthermore, men had slightly higher levels of addictive SMU and loneliness; in contrast, women had slightly higher levels of offline social support. Thus, persons of both genders who tend to addictive SMU could be at risk for enhanced loneliness when they perceive little social support offline. Potential ways how to protect this group against this negative effect of the online activity are discussed.

Dark personality traits and online toxicity: Linking self-reports to Reddit activity
abstract: Dark personality traits have long been associated with antisocial and toxic online behaviors, yet their relationship with observable online activity remains unclear. We investigate the association between validated dark personality measures, self-reported experiences of online incivility, and linguistic and behavioral features extracted from real-world user activity. To this end, we developed a Web application that securely links responses to validated psychological questionnaires collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk with participants’ Reddit activity. This yielded a dataset of nearly 57K comments (2.2M tokens) from 114 users, represented through a broad set of linguistic and behavioral features. Our analyses reveal a clear distinction between self-reported and observed behavior. Dark personality traits show consistent associations with self-reported engagement in uncivil interactions. However, no validated dark personality dimension significantly predicts text-derived toxicity or linguistic features. In contrast, self-reported experiences of engaging in or being targeted by toxic behavior are robustly reflected in users’ language, exhibiting consistent associations with measures of negativity, moral framing, and emotional intensity. Taken together, these findings highlight a gap between stable personality traits and their manifestation in surface-level linguistic signals. While computational features effectively capture behavioral engagement in online incivility, they do not provide reliable proxies for underlying personality constructs within the present framework. Our results underscore the importance of grounding computational approaches in validated psychological measures and point to the need for richer, context-aware representations to better understand the relationship between personality and online behavior.

title: Virtual proxemics “in the wild”: a cross-cultural comparison between Japanese and Italian adults recruited at public fairs
abstract: People regulate comfort and intimacy of everyday social interactions by adjusting interpersonal distance- the physical space between themselves and others. While research has highlighted the role of cultural norms in shaping interpersonal distance, their modulation during intergroup encounters remains underexplored. Immersive virtual reality (IVR) offers a powerful platform for simulating intergroup encounters by enabling embodied, repeatable interactions while controlling the appearance and behaviours of social targets. In this study, we capitalized on portable IVR that enables data collection “in the wild”, to examine how group membership influences interpersonal distance in Japanese and Italian people, often characterized as non-contact and contact cultures, respectively. One hundred eighty-four participants were immersed in a virtual reality scenario and asked to adjust their preferred interpersonal distance from Asian and Caucasian virtual agents. Participants also reported explicit attitudes toward ingroup and outgroup members and completed a Brief Implicit Association Test. Japanese participants preferred larger interpersonal distances than Italian participants. Higher perceived attractiveness and trustworthiness predicted shorter preferred distances, and these effects were consistent across samples. Moreover, stronger pro-Caucasian implicit bias was associated with maintaining a greater distance from Asian (vs. Caucasian) agents. These findings show that differences in proxemic behavior between Japanese and Italian participants, together with implicit bias, may shape interpersonal spacing in virtual environments, with potential implications for intergroup relations in immersive social interactions that can be foreseen to happen in the near future.

title: Enhancing human detection of real and hyperrealistic AI-generated faces
abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) have prompted concern about the proliferation of deepfake content—synthetic images, audio, and videos—online. StyleGAN2-generated images of White human faces are especially problematic, as people often perceive them as more real than real human faces—a phenomenon known as AI hyperrealism . Across four preregistered experiments ( N = 661), we developed and tested DISCERN-AI, a novel behavioral intervention that combines feature-based instructions with inductive category learning to enhance human discrimination between real and StyleGAN2 faces. Participants consistently showed above-chance discrimination performance following the intervention, including after a 20-day delay. Overall, the results suggest that category learning regimes, such as DISCERN-AI, can be effective tools for improving human detection of synthetic facial images.

The impact of affordances for emotional human–chatbot interaction on users’ willingness to self-disclose
abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence, chatbots are increasingly transitioning from instrumental tools toward emotionally interactive “communicators,” and users’ self-disclosure behavior is becoming more prevalent. To uncover the underlying mechanisms of this behavior, this study innovatively introduces the integrative construct of affordances for emotional human–chatbot interaction, conceptualized across five dimensions: perceived cognitive ability, empathetic ability, companionship ability, security, and controllability. With social presence as a mediator, the research systematically examines how these affordances shape users’ willingness to self-disclose. Based on a survey of 541 Generation Z users with chatbot experience, the findings reveal that empathetic ability, companionship ability, security, and cognitive ability all significantly and positively predicted willingness to self-disclose. Social presence played a partial or complete mediating role in these relationships. Controllability, however, showed no significant effect, reflecting an inherent tension between “control” and “immersion” in emotional interaction. Theoretically, this study extends affordance theory into the domain of affective interaction from a dynamic, human–AI co-construction perspective, offering an integrated analytical framework for understanding the formation of social relationships with AI. Practically, it provides empirical evidence and actionable insights for the design and ethical implementation of emotionally aware AI systems.

The work-related consequences of employees’ media-based political information consumption: A nine-wave weekly study during the 2024 U.S. presidential primary season
abstract: To cope with political stress, many people spend considerable time seeking political information. Indeed, whether on social media sites (e.g., Facebook) or through traditional outlets like television, people consume political information as a means of staying updated about political issues that have the potential to affect them and their communities. Considering the pervasive effects of politics, might the valence and frequency of political information consumed in the nonwork domain have implications for their behavior at work? The purpose of the present research was to examine the influence of consuming media-based negative and positive political information outside of work on employee behavior (i.e., political correctness, helping behavior) and engagement at work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we propose that during weeks when employees consume more negative and positive political information outside of work than their usual, they experience increased anxiety and hope, respectively. We further posit that these cognitive–affective states shape work-related outcomes, promoting resource-preserving behaviors (e.g., reduced work engagement, heightened political correctness) and resource-investing behaviors (e.g., increased helping and engagement). To test these hypotheses, we used a nine-wave weekly sample of U.S. workers collected during the 2024 U.S. Presidential Primaries (i.e., from January 19 th through March 15 th ; N Weeks = 2,772, N Employees = 308). Multilevel path analyses of these data largely supported our hypotheses.

title: Mindfulness training in virtual reality for Borderline Personality Disorder symptoms: An analogue study
abstract: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a severe, complex condition that has significant adverse effects on the physical, social, and economic well-being of patients. The mindfulness skills training module of Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DPT) as a stand-alone treatment is an effective treatment for BPD. However, borderline patients often fail to engage in mindfulness interventions due to struggles with concentration. Virtual Reality (VR) is a new modality for the administration of mindfulness training that holds great potential in increasing engagement and access, however whether the effects of virtual environments can match that of real scenarios and traditional mindfulness practices for BPD symptoms remains unknown. In Study 1, participants (N = 58) listened to a pre-recorded mindfulness audio while either looking at a virtual green space or a real green space in a single session. In Study 2, participants (N = 26) listened to the recording under three conditions (audio-only, audio and real green space, and audio and virtual green space) and underwent three mindfulness sessions. Measures of BPD symptoms and mindfulness skills were obtained pre- and post-sessions, and at one-week follow-up in Study 1 and two-week follow up in Study 2. Results from both studies showed a significant reduction in the same BPD measure and increase in mindfulness from pre- to post-intervention, with no significant difference among conditions. This effect was mostly maintained at the follow-up. Results of both studies suggest that VR interventions including DBT based mindfulness skills training could be effectively exploited to reduce BPD symptoms by enhancing accessibility, increasing engagement and avoiding dropouts.

Substratism: Conceptualizing and measuring moral bias against AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems (AIs) are increasingly taking on social roles, such as virtual coworkers and personal companions. Yet people grant AIs little moral concern, even when they are described as indistinguishable from humans. We conceptualize this bias as substratism: the moral devaluation of AIs based on the non-biological substrate that underlies their cognitive processes and makes up their broader physical form (e.g., silicon and wires rather than flesh and blood). Across five preregistered studies (N = 2,129), we introduce substratism as a psychological construct and develop and validate a scale to measure it. In Study 1, we found that substratism is best captured by a unidimensional factor structure, and we reduced a large initial item pool into an eight-item scale. Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the scale’s factor structure with independent samples and showed that substratism is correlated with some AI-related beliefs and behaviors, such as perceived threat from AI and interaction with AI. However, it is weakly correlated or uncorrelated with other prejudices and their underlying causes, suggesting that substratism has some unique psychological explanations. Studies 4 and 5 showed that substratism predicts relevant outcomes: prioritizing humans and non-human animals over AIs in moral dilemmas and charity donation decisions, and choosing to learn about an AI rights charity and its petition. Overall, our findings suggest that substratism is a distinct, measurable construct that varies widely across individuals, and we provide a concise, validated scale to capture and quantify this bias against increasingly advanced AI systems.

AI disclosure formats and user responses to AI-generated video: Evidence from a cross-national experiment
abstract: As AI-generated media becomes more common, transparency policies frequently require the disclosure of synthetic content. However, little is known about how different warning formats influence perceived accuracy, midpoint or ambivalent responses, and observable behavioral engagement across cultural contexts. We conducted a multi-country experiment (5435 participants; 43,512 video-level observations) spanning five countries (the United States, Japan, Germany, France, and Indonesia) and comparing two disclosure formats: a pre-exposure message-style warning and an embedded label-style disclosure. Message-style warnings significantly reduced perceived accuracy but did not increase perceived differentiation between true and false videos. In contrast, label-style disclosures increased midpoint responses, consistent with greater expressed uncertainty or ambivalence, but did not increase observable behavioral engagement or perceived differentiation between true and false videos. Across models, individual differences, including attitudes toward AI, conspiracy beliefs, trust in social media, and personality traits (Openness to Experience, Agreeableness, and Extraversion), were substantially stronger predictors of perceived accuracy than warning format. Cross-national differences also exceeded intervention effects. These findings suggest that AI transparency cues primarily modulate perceived accuracy and confidence expression rather than improve veracity-contingent evaluative differentiation. Overall, the disclosure effects were modest relative to individual differences, psychological orientations, and country-level variation. Therefore, AI disclosure systems should be evaluated not only by visibility but also by how they shape multiple user responses under different informational contexts.

title: Fake or trustworthy? A TCCM- and bibliometric-based hybrid review of online review research
The creative tax of videoconferencing: How ideological diversity mitigates creativity losses in virtual teams
abstract: ABSTRACT Videoconferencing has become a central medium for collaboration in contemporary organizations, yet mounting evidence suggests that it can carry a "creative tax" that is associated with lower idea generation. Building on information decision-making perspectives and the categorization elaboration model, we argue that team heterogeneity can partially offset this creativity loss in virtual teams. In a laboratory experiment with 415 participants organized into 86 teams, we compared randomly assigned face-to-face teams with self-selected virtual teams collaborating via Zoom. Teams completed a 15-minute brainstorming task and selected a focal idea, which was later evaluated on multiple quality dimensions by independent judges. As expected, virtual teams produced significantly lower quality ideas than face-to-face teams. Because virtual teams self-selected whereas face-to-face teams were randomly assigned, these effects reflect associations within our design rather than causal effects of modality. However, both surface-level (gender and nationality) and deep-level (religiosity and political orientation) heterogeneity were positively associated with idea quality, with political diversity emerging as the strongest predictor. Mediation analyses further showed that the negative effect of videoconferencing on creative performance was partly explained by the higher homogeneity of self-selected virtual teams. Together, these findings refine theory on team diversity and computer-mediated collaboration by highlighting deep-level ideological diversity as an immediate cognitive counterweight to the attentional narrowing inherent in screen-mediated interaction. They also offer practical guidance for designing virtual and hybrid work practices, suggesting that diverse team composition is a key design lever for preserving creativity in videoconference-based teamwork.
